alpha_d_glucopyranose.name: α-D-Glucopyranose
alpha_d_glucopyranose.caption: The hemiacetal –OH that C1 gains sits on the face opposite the C5 CH₂OH — the α form.

beta_d_glucopyranose.name: β-D-Glucopyranose
beta_d_glucopyranose.caption: Same ring and same four centres; the C1 –OH now shares a face with the C5 CH₂OH — the β form.

alpha_d_fructofuranose.name: α-D-Fructofuranose
alpha_d_fructofuranose.caption: A five-membered ring: the anomeric carbon is C2, carrying an –OH and the CH₂OH that C1 became.

beta_d_fructofuranose.name: β-D-Fructofuranose
beta_d_fructofuranose.caption: At C2 the –OH and CH₂OH sit on opposite faces from the α anomer — the whole α/β difference.

sucrose.name: Sucrose
sucrose.caption: One oxygen bridges C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose, so neither anomeric centre is free — hence non-reducing.

maltose.name: Maltose
maltose.caption: The C1→C4 link uses up only one anomeric carbon; the second ring keeps its own, which is why maltose reduces.

glycyl_l_alanine.name: Glycyl-L-alanine
glycyl_l_alanine.caption: Glycine supplies the –COOH and alanine the –NH₂, leaving one –CO–NH– between the two α-carbons.

beta_d_ribofuranose.name: β-D-Ribofuranose
beta_d_ribofuranose.caption: RNA's sugar: –OH groups on C2′ and C3′ as well as C5′, all on the same five-membered ring.

beta_d_deoxyribofuranose.name: 2-Deoxy-β-D-ribofuranose
beta_d_deoxyribofuranose.caption: The identical ring with only hydrogens on C2′ — the one missing –OH that separates DNA from RNA.
